claim: No tournament on 51 or fewer vertices has S_4, so f(4) >= 52. For A = N^-(v) in Corollary 3, sum_z |D_z| equals sum_{x in A}(d^+(x) - 1). Every inference on the printed path follows. There is no first failing inference and no unfinished block on that path. Erdős problem 902 is not solved.
definitions: A tournament has one directed edge between every two distinct vertices. D(X) is the set of vertices outside X that beat every vertex of X. S_4 means every 4-set has a nonempty dominator set. f(4) is the least order of a tournament with S_4. A pair P is tight when |D(P)| = 11. For r in R = D(P), write d^-(r) = 25 + j_r and J(P) = sum j_r. Z is the set of vertices of in-degree 24, and e(x) = d^-(x) - 25. For v in Z and A = N^-(v), and for each of the other 50 vertices z, D_z = D({v, z}) and h_z = |D_z| - 11. W is the sum over x in A of max(e(x), 0). A tournament on 51 vertices is doubly regular when every in-degree and every out-degree is 25 and every pair has exactly 12 common in-neighbours. Lemma J is the bound J >= 3 for every tight pair; on 51 vertices it is Theorem 1 of proof/F4_GE_52_HAND_PROOF.md.
argument:
Answer to the assigned checks. The identity in Corollary 3 holds. Each x in A = N^-(v) has v as an out-neighbour, so the out-neighbours of x among the other 50 vertices are exactly the remaining d^+(x) - 1 out-neighbours. Those are the vertices z for which x lies in D_z. Therefore sum_z |D_z| = sum_{x in A}(d^+(x) - 1). At order 51, d^+(x) = 50 - d^-(x), so the same sum is sum_x (49 - d^-(x)) = 24*49 - sum d^-(x) = 1176 - sum d^-(x). Subtracting 50*11 = 550 gives sum h_z = 626 - sum_{x in A} d^-(x), which is the printed formula. No inference on the path from the basic lemmas through Theorem 5 fails. The path was finished. The paragraph that begins 'Theorem 1 holds for every N' is not on this path.

Block A, orders at most 50. Lemmas 1.1-1.3 of proof/ERDOS902_PROOF.md give (F1)-(F3). If a vertex outside D(A) beat every vertex of D(A), the set A union that vertex would have a dominator inside D(A), and the two edges between them cannot both exist. So every triple has at least 5 dominators, every pair has at least 11, and the in-neighbourhood of a tight pair induces a 5-regular tournament on 11 vertices. Lemma T: the 45 triples of R through a fixed r contribute at least 225 dominator incidences; the five in-neighbours inside R contribute 30; each of the other d^-(r) - 5 in-neighbours beats at most six vertices of R and hence at most C(5, 2) = 10 of the triples. Thus 225 <= 30 + 10(d^-(r) - 5), so d^-(r) >= 24.5, and an integer in-degree is at least 25. If some in-degree equals 23, the in-neighbourhood A is 11-regular of order 23, every pair {a, v} with a in A is tight, and Lemma T lifts every in-degree in A to at least 25. Arcs from A into the out-neighbourhood then give 11(N - 24) <= 23(N - 38), hence N >= 51. At order at most 50 every in-degree is therefore at least 24. The handshaking bound forces order at least 49. The excess sum (d^- - 24) equals 0 at order 49 and 25 at order 50, so the set Z of in-degree 24 has size 49 or at least 25. Claim Q forbids that. Inside an in-neighbourhood of order 24 the internal in-degrees are 11 + f_x with sum f = 12, so at least 12 vertices give a tight pair with the apex. Each such vertex beats every other vertex of Z in that neighbourhood, so at most one of them lies in Z. The remaining vertices of Z in the neighbourhood are beaten by all of those tight vertices, and the resulting quadratic form (q - 1)(ell - 12) + C(q, 2) is positive for q >= 2. Thus each vertex of Z has at most two in-neighbours in Z, so |Z| <= 5. Orders 49 and 50 are impossible, and so is every smaller order. This is Theorem A: f(4) >= 51 if an S_4 tournament exists at all, and in any case no S_4 tournament has 50 or fewer vertices.

Block B, Theorem 1 at order 51. Let P be tight, R = D(P), and O the remaining 38 vertices. The out-neighbour count gives exactly 20 + j_r vertices of O that beat a given r, and sum_y (q_y - 5) = 8 - J. The triple count through r rearranges to sum lambda(q_y) <= 5 + 10 j_r, where lambda(5, 6, 7, 8, 9) = 0, 4, 7, 9, 10 and lambda is 10 for every larger admissible q. Lambda is nonnegative for q >= 5, so one vertex of q = 7 forces four positive j-values and one of q = 8 forces three. Under J <= 2 every q_y lies in {5, 6} or is at least 9. The global triple count 110 + sum C(11 - q_y, 3) >= 825 then becomes 20m + 10 n_6 <= 45, while the excess identity forces n_6 + sum_{q >= 9}(q - 5) >= 6. The only surviving profile is one vertex y* with q >= 9, at most two vertices with q = 6, and every other vertex of O with q = 5. In that profile the pair excess is s(u, v) = 3c(u, v) + 4k(u, v) + 3m(u, v) - 45: each common in-neighbour in R covers three further vertices of R, a 5-vertex that beats both endpoints covers four, a 6-vertex covers three, and y* covers none. Summing and using alpha = 20 + j - beta - gamma produces sum_v s(u, v) = 10 + 20 j_u - 8 beta_u - 20 gamma_u. Modulo 4, s is congruent to 3 - c - m. Since s >= 0 and c + m <= 6, the least admissible value is 3 - c - m when c + m <= 3, and 7 - c - m when c + m >= 4. Summing those bounds yields beta_u + 5 gamma_u + N_4(u) <= 5 j_u. A vertex of excess 0 therefore lies in Q_{y*} and in every 6-set Q_y, and has c <= 3. A 6-vertex would then miss five vertices, all outside the excess-zero set, but that set omits at most J <= 2 vertices. So there is no 6-vertex, the excess identity forces J = 2 and Q_{y*} = R, and every other vertex of O has q = 5. For an excess-zero vertex the same bounds collapse to equalities and give |D({u, v})| = 12 for every other v. For an arbitrary s the same description gives sum_{v != s} |D({s, v})| = 120 + 5 j_s. One vertex of excess 2 then has pair-sum 120 against the required 130. Two vertices of excess 1 force the pair they span to have 17 dominators and pair excess 23 - c >= 19, while the 45 triples through one of them have total excess 15 and the nine triples through both are a nonnegative part of that total. Both shapes are impossible, so J >= 3. The argument never uses the edge inside P, the in-degrees of the two vertices of P, or the isomorphism type of T[R].

Block C, Corollary 2. Suppose d^-(v) = 23 at order 51. The same regularity count as in Lemma 2.2 makes every pair {a, v} with a in N^-(v) tight, and Lemma T gives e >= 0 on that in-neighbourhood. Arcs into the 27-vertex out-neighbourhood number at least 11*27 = 297 and exactly 299 - sum e, so the excess over A is at most 2. The dominators of any tight pair {a, v} lie in A and have nonnegative excess, so J <= 2, contradicting Theorem 1. Every in-degree is at least 24.

Block D, Corollary 3. The average in-degree is 25. If Z is nonempty, fix v in Z and A = N^-(v). The Gram matrix G of the 50 indicator vectors of the sets D_z has rank at most 24, so in decreasing order its eigenvalues satisfy lambda_i(G) = 0 for every i >= 25. The off-diagonal entries are at least 5, and M = G - 5*11^T has diagonal 6 + h_z and nonnegative off-diagonal entries. The largest eigenvalue of -5*11^T is 0, so Weyl's inequality gives lambda_i(M) <= lambda_i(G). Hence M has at least 26 eigenvalues less than or equal to 0. From the arc identity and d^- = 25 + e, the sum of d^- over A equals 600 - q + W, where q = |A intersect Z| is at most 2 by Claim Q. Therefore sum h_z = 26 + q - W <= 28 - W. The number n_t of positive h_z is at most that sum. If h_z = 0, the off-diagonal sum of row z of M equals sum_{y in O}(q_y - 5) = 8 - J({v, z}) by the same identity (I2) used for Theorem 1, because the eleven contributions inside R are in-degrees of a 5-regular tournament minus 5. Theorem 1 makes this sum at most 5, which is strictly less than the diagonal entry 6. The omitted entries of a principal submatrix are nonnegative, so the principal submatrix on the tight indices is strictly diagonally dominant with positive diagonal. Its eigenvalues are real and at least 1. Cauchy interlacing then gives M at least 50 - n_t positive eigenvalues. At most 24 eigenvalues can be positive, so n_t >= 26. Combined with n_t <= 26 + q - W this forces W <= q <= 2. Claim Q supplies a tight pair {a, v} whose dominators lie in A and have nonnegative excess, so its J is at most W, hence at most 2, contradicting Theorem 1. Case (I) is impossible.

Block E, Corollary 4 and Theorem 5. Every in-degree is 25. A tight pair would have J = 0. Theorem 1 forbids that, so every pair has at least 12 dominators. The sum of |D(P)| equals 51*C(25, 2) = 15300 = 12*C(51, 2), so every pair has exactly 12 dominators. If u beats w, the 24 in-neighbours of w other than u consist of the 12 common in-neighbours of {u, w} and 12 out-neighbours of u; the other 12 out-neighbours of u besides w are then common out-neighbours. For a triple Y, inclusion-exclusion on the 48 vertices outside Y gives |D(Y)| + |D^+(Y)| = 12 - sigma(Y): the three in-neighbourhoods contribute 72 outside Y, and the third vertex of Y is a dominator of exactly sigma(Y) of the three pairs. There are 15300 transitive triples and 5525 cyclic triples. Each out-neighbourhood induces a 12-regular tournament on 25 vertices, with 1650 transitive triples and 650 cyclic triples, so the sums of k are 84150 and 33150. The means are 11/2 and 6. Counting triples inside the 12 common out-neighbours of a pair gives sum C(k, 2) = 280500. Counting pairs of triples with all six edges forward gives sum C(k, 3) = sum C(12 - sigma - k, 3). If k >= 5, the centred variables u sum to 0 on each class, and the cubic identity collapses to the sum of all u^3 being 0. Then sum (u^3 - u/4) over transitive triples plus sum (u^3 - u) over cyclic triples is 0. Under k >= 5 every summand is nonnegative, so each is zero: transitive triples have 5 or 6 dominators and cyclic triples have 5, 6, or 7. The means force 7650 transitive triples of each kind, and equally many cyclic triples with 5 and with 7 dominators. The second-moment sum is then 274125 + p with p = 6375. But 2p <= 5525. This contradiction shows that some triple has at most 4 dominators.

Assembly. Theorem A excludes every order at most 50. An S_4 tournament on 51 vertices would be doubly regular by Corollary 4 and would then have a triple with at most 4 dominators, contradicting (F1). The same chain uses S_4 only through (F1), so every tournament on at most 51 vertices, whether or not it has S_4, has a triple with at most 4 dominators. Thus f(4) >= 52. The upper bound f(4) <= 67 is not part of the argument and was not re-proved. Erdős problem 902 is not solved.

evidence.block_not_on_the_path: The paragraph beginning 'Theorem 1 holds for every N' was not used. R1-G already found its printed citation of (R1)-(R3) incomplete. The N=51 proof does not cite it.

weaknesses: The status proved is the nonexistence of an S_4 tournament on at most 51 vertices, together with the resulting lower bound f(4) >= 52. It is not a solution of Erdős problem 902. The classical upper bound f(4) <= 67 was not re-proved, so this pass does not identify f(4). Order 52 was not considered. Weyl's inequality, Gershgorin's theorem, and Cauchy interlacing are used as standard facts about Hermitian matrices; their hypotheses were checked in the decreasing eigenvalue convention, and they were not re-proved from the characteristic polynomial. The every-order paragraph after Theorem 1 remains an incomplete citation, as previously reported, and the structural sentence about an arbitrary tight dominator of in-degree 25 was not given a separate proof here because Corollary 2, Corollary 3, and Corollary 4 do not use it. No tournament was enumerated.
next_step: Leave the bound f(4) >= 52 as checked and unreviewed, and do not record Erdős problem 902 as solved. The next mathematical question is order 52: whether an S_4 tournament there can avoid a tight pair, and whether a tight pair at that order can be excluded. This pass does not start that case.
relation_to_prior: The chain had been read and not promoted. R1-G proved J >= 3 at every order by a repaired argument and explicitly did not certify the N=51 write-up of Theorem 1. This pass certifies that write-up and then uses it. R1-B proved the third-moment bound for a tournament that is already doubly regular; Corollaries 2-4 are the reduction to that hypothesis, which R1-H listed as the first unchecked obstacle. The arc identity was recomputed from the definition, not taken from the random trials. The exhausted approach keys were not used.
novelty: The new content is the check that the printed path does not break. The mod-4 case split and the third-moment comparison are the printed arguments. What had not been recorded is that sum |D_z| really is sum (d^+(x) - 1), that this gives the exact excess sum 26 + |A intersect Z| - W, and that the nonnegative off-diagonal entries let the full row-sum bound of 5 pass to the tight principal submatrix. With that estimate, W <= 2 and the tight pair inside A contradicts J >= 3. No earlier inference fails.
